newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta beaten lower by dollar fall, EMU jitters.
newsitem.headline: Peseta beaten lower by dollar fall, EMU jitters.

text.p: The peseta weakened sharply against the mark on Tuesday, beaten lower by the dollar's steep slide and jitters that Germany may not meet the Maastricht criteria, analysts said.
"We've broken strong resistance at 84.30 and now we're heading for 84.50," one trader said.

"That should hold for the time being, but that depends of course on whether the dollar falls much further," said another trader, adding that he expected the Bank of Spain to break the Spanish currency's fall if it weakened much further.
Analysts said the dollar's steep fall against the mark and yen ahead of a run of U.S. economic data this week had sent the peseta on a downward spin.
"The movements in the dollar against the mark have affected practically all the markets," said one trader.
This week's data from the world's biggest economy start with third-quarter employment cost and consumer confidence figures on on Tuesday and culminate in October payrolls data on Friday.
"This week we've got some important data from the U.S. and their effect on the dollar will be fundamental," said one dealer.
Friday's unemployment data and preliminary third-quarter gross domestic product data due on Wednesday would be the most closely watched, he said.

The peseta also suffered pressure from a rising mark after Germany's six leading economic research institutes said a slight monetary tightening was possible if growth in money supply stayed above target levels.

The institutes said Germany would fail to meet strict debt and deficit criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1997, boosting the mark further. Next year will be key for deciding what countries will participate in EMU at the scheduled start in January 1999.
But analysts said that EMU factors were not the prime focus for the peseta's fall.
"The market is not focused on EMU at the moment, it's focus is the dollar move. There's still confidence that EMU will happen," said one trader.

Some traders said they expected the Bank of Spain to try to brake the peseta's fall, intervening at around 84.45. At 1130 GMT, the peseta was trading at 84.30/31 per mark, near its level at the beginning of September.
But other analysts said 85.00 peseta/mark was a more realistic level.

"The Bank of Spain is unlikely to defend the peseta at these levels as they will be delighted to see a weakening in the currency toward 85.00 or even 86.00," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
